opus-5.5.text:
I think that view is understandable, but I'd push back on it pretty strongly. It's true that Transformers have been remarkably general. You can throw them at language, images, audio, proteins, and they tend to work. That's a real achievement, and I don't want to downplay it. But "works well" and "solved" are very different claims.

For one thing, a lot of what we attribute to the Transformer is really the result of scale: more data, more compute, and an enormous amount of engineering effort that's gone into optimizing that one architecture. When an entire field pours its resources into a single design for years, of course it's going to look dominant. That doesn't necessarily tell you it's the best possible point in the design space. It might just be the one we've explored most thoroughly.

And there are concrete limitations that haven't gone away. The most obvious one is efficiency. Attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and at inference time you have this KV cache that grows linearly with context. That becomes a real bottleneck when you care about very long sequences, like long documents, genomics, high-resolution audio or video, or agents that need to maintain state over long interactions. People have built a lot of clever workarounds, but they're workarounds.

Then there's a more conceptual point. Attention is essentially a mechanism that keeps everything around and looks back over it. That's very powerful for certain kinds of recall, but it's not obviously how you'd want a system to compress and reason over information in general. Recurrent or state space approaches make a different tradeoff. They maintain a compressed state, which is more efficient and arguably closer to how you'd want a system to process a continuous stream of data. Each approach has strengths and weaknesses, and I think understanding those tradeoffs, and how to combine them, is where a lot of the interesting work is. We've already seen hybrid models that mix attention with recurrent layers do really well.

There's also the question of the inductive biases baked into things like tokenization. A lot of the pipeline around Transformers, like how we chunk data into tokens, is a kind of hand-engineered preprocessing that I think should eventually be learned end to end. That's an architectural question too.

So my view is that we're actually still pretty early. The Transformer was a huge step, but I'd be surprised if, ten years from now, we looked back and said that was the final answer. Architecture research is still very much alive, and there's a lot left to figure out.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts attention with recurrent and state space approaches, explaining their different strengths for recall, long sequences, and continuous streams.

r002.rationale: It attributes Transformers’ dominance to scale, compute, and engineering effort. Its mention of tokenization does not say that widespread use partly reflects transforming data into forms suited to Transformers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I hear that a lot, and I think it's kind of an overstatement, maybe even a category error. The Transformer is an incredibly good architecture, I'm not going to argue with that. Attention is a really powerful primitive, it's hardware-friendly, it scales, and it's been validated across language, vision, audio, you name it. So in some sense the empirical success speaks for itself.

But I'd push back on the word "solved." When people say that, what they usually mean is that the Transformer is good enough that further architectural work has diminishing returns compared to just scaling data and compute. And that's a reasonable bet for a certain regime. The problem is that it conflates "works well" with "optimal," and those are really different claims.

If you look at what attention actually does, it's a very specific inductive bias. It's a lossless cache of every token you've seen, and you pay quadratic compute and linear memory for the privilege of looking back at all of it. That's great for some things, like exact retrieval or in-context lookup over tokenized text. But it's also a pretty weird way to model a lot of data. If you think about raw audio, or DNA, or long multimodal streams, the information isn't neatly packaged into discrete semantic units the way words are. Tokenization is doing an enormous amount of work for the Transformer, and I'd argue a lot of the "architecture is solved" story is really "tokenization plus attention is a good match for text."

The other thing I'd say is that the architecture question has been reframed, not closed. The interesting question to me isn't "Transformer or not Transformer," it's what are the tradeoffs between different ways of compressing context. State space models, or more broadly recurrent and linear-attention style models, make a different tradeoff: they compress history into a fixed-size state. You lose perfect recall, but you gain constant-memory inference and the ability to process really long sequences. And it turns out that for a lot of tasks that compression is not a bug, it's a feature, because it forces the model to learn what matters. Hybrids that mix the two end up being better than either alone, which to me is pretty strong evidence that neither is the final answer.

There's also a more practical point. Even if the Transformer were the end of the road for modeling quality, inference cost is a huge driver of what gets deployed, and that's an architectural question. A lot of the efficiency work people are doing right now, from KV cache compression to speculative decoding to distilling attention into recurrent layers, is implicitly admitting that the architecture isn't settled. We're just doing it piecemeal instead of calling it architecture research.

So my honest assessment is: the Transformer is a local optimum that happens to be very good and very well-tuned, and we've poured enormous engineering effort into making it fast. That creates a strong gravitational pull. But I think there's a lot of room left, especially once you move beyond text, beyond short contexts, and once you start asking what a model should do with its memory instead of just assuming it should remember everything. I'd actually say architecture research is more interesting now than it was five years ago, precisely because we have a strong baseline to compare against.

r001.rationale: The response says attention and tokenization are a good match for text but a poor fit for some raw or long-sequence data, and describes state-space and recurrent models as offering different tradeoffs for those sequences.

r002.rationale: It says tokenization does substantial work for Transformers and that their success partly reflects “tokenization plus attention” being a good match for text.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think architecture is solved. Transformers work remarkably well across a lot of tasks, and that’s strong evidence that they’re a very useful architecture. But that’s different from saying they’re the best way to do everything, or that there aren’t meaningful improvements left to make.

One way I think about this is to ask how a model handles information as a sequence gets longer. Attention lets you look back at everything in the context, which is very powerful, but it also comes with a cost. A recurrent model takes a different approach: it compresses the past into a state. That can be much more efficient, but then you have to figure out what information to retain. Those are real architectural tradeoffs.

And architecture interacts with scale, hardware, and the task you care about. Something that works best in one setting might not work best in another. So I’d say Transformers have given us a very strong starting point. I wouldn’t take their success as a reason to stop exploring alternatives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architectural tradeoffs across tasks and settings, but does not state that architectures suit different types of data.

r002.rationale: It says Transformers work well across many tasks, but does not explain their widespread use as partly resulting from transforming data into Transformer-suited forms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s too strong a claim. Transformers work very well, and they’ve shown that you can use one architecture across a surprisingly broad range of tasks. But that doesn’t mean architecture is solved. It means we’ve found a very good architecture, especially for the settings where we’ve invested the most effort.

An architecture makes choices about how information is represented and how it moves through the model. Those choices affect what the model can learn, how efficiently it learns it, and how expensive it is to run. Even if two architectures eventually reach similar performance, needing substantially less computation or memory would be a meaningful improvement.

So I’d separate the claim that Transformers are a strong general-purpose approach from the claim that there’s nothing left to discover. We should keep asking where their limitations are, and whether different architectural choices give us better tradeoffs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses architectural tradeoffs and limitations, but does not state that different architectures suit different types of data.

r002.rationale: It does not say that Transformers’ widespread use partly comes from transforming data into forms suited to them.
